Therefore, this section focuses on 15-minute time-series data for those end uses across the three example units. Heating end uses include space heating, heating fans and pumps, heat pump backup heating, and any associated backup fans or pumps. Cooling end uses include space cooling and cooling fans or pumps. January 2 and July 2 were selected to represent typical winter and summer days for analyzing heating and cooling loads, respectively. Figure 6 shows that for unit 1 in Florida (climate zone 1A), hot-humid climate, the example dwelling unit uses electricity for both heating and cooling. As shown in the top panel of Figure 6, the attic insulation upgrade reduces cooling energy consumption during the afternoon hours when outdoor temperatures are highest. The improved attic insulation lowers heat gain, resulting in less demand on the cooling system. On the winter day (bottom panel), heating energy use remains near zero throughout the day. This is consistent with the minimal heating demand typical of zone 1A, where 28% of homes in Florida either don’t have or don’t use heating equipment [12]. These results show that while insulation has limited effect on heating in warm climates, it does help reduce summer cooling loads. 11 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
